records.message: MapleStar, you say you "lean toward thinking some mandates" might be necessary, but you didn't see my grandmother, Elara, 78, vibrant and stubborn, arguing politics with me just hours before. I found her on the kitchen floor, her hand cold, the radio still playing her favorite jazz. The coroner’s report listed “coincidental heart failure” and closed the case without a second thought. Your policy leanings feel like a betrayal when the system so casually writes off her life as collateral damage.

All these stories are exactly why I’m stuck. I don’t think the answer is to throw out vaccines entirely—they obviously do a lot of good. But handing the power to mandate them to a system that responds to real harm with a shrug and a ‘coincidence’ form letter? That’s a hard pass from me. It feels like we’re asking people to trust a process that has shown it won’t trust them back when it matters most.

Yeah, you're pinpointing the real issue. It's the trust gap. If the system had a better, more transparent way to investigate and support the rare cases, more people would probably accept mandates when they're truly necessary. Right now, it feels like we have to choose between two flawed options.

You're right about the trust issue. Once you've been on the receiving end of that 'coincidence' line from an official, it's hard to ever take their word at face value again. I get why people would resist a mandate if they think the system will abandon them the second something goes wrong.

I can't even begin to process the pain in your story, and you're right—the 'coincidence' dismissal is the worst part. It completely erodes trust. Maybe that's the real question here: not just if we should have mandates, but can we build a system that's actually accountable when the rare, terrible thing happens? Because without that, any mandate feels cruel, no matter what the math says.
